meaning: Son of the sea (from Old Irish Manannán)

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial nasal [m], broad — the plain 'm' of English 'man'.
Short open [a], the unstressed first vowel; Old Irish carries its stress at the front of the word.
Broad nasal [n̪ˠ], short open [a], and a second broad [n̪ˠ] — the doubled letter the medieval spelling keeps.
Long open [aː] marked by the síneadh fada, closing the name with a broad [n̪ˠ] — the length the temple's Tier 1 rests on.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MAH-nuh-nawn' — stress the first syllable, keep the middle vowels short and plain, and lengthen the final 'awn'. The Anglicized retellings say 'man-ə-NAWN'; Old Irish would not have.

pronunciation.note: Manannan is Tier 1 by the mechanical rule: the temple form Manannán carries a síneadh fada on the final á, a distinctive feature plain ASCII strips. The name is traditionally explained as 'son of the sea' (mac Lir), and the reconstruction marks initial stress, as Old Irish demands; the double n simply belongs to the medieval spelling.

domains.title: Lord of the Sea and Mist
domains.subtitle: Guardian of the Irish Otherworld
domains.lead: Manannán mac Lir — 'son of the Sea', glossed so in Sanas Cormaic — is the great god of the wave, the mist, and the threshold. He rules the waters and weather around Ireland, keeps the Land of Promise hidden behind the féth fíada, and acts as foster-father and quartermaster to the Túatha Dé Danann — appearing where the known world ends to explain what lies beyond it.

cards.name: Sea Lord
cards.desc: The sea took its name from him or he from it — Sanas Cormaic glosses Manannán as mac mara, 'son of the sea' — and the waters and weather around Ireland answer to him.

cards.name: Otherworld Guardian
cards.desc: The féth fíada, the cloak of mist, hides Tír Tairngire and the hollow hills from mortal eyes — and it is his.

cards.name: Treasure-Giver
cards.desc: He arms the heroes: Fragarach the Answerer, the horse Aonbharr, the boat Sguaba Tuinne, the crane-bag that opens only at the full of the tide.

cards.name: Shape-Shifter
cards.desc: He comes as warrior, fisherman, and grey-haired beggar — in Echtra Cormaic an old man with a staff leads the king through the mist to the Land of Promise.

symbols.name: Boat Sguaba Tuinne
symbols.meaning: The Wave-sweeper, a self-propelling boat that obeyed its owner's thought and needed neither sail nor oar

symbols.name: Horse Aonbharr
symbols.meaning: The steed that travelled over land and sea alike, swifter than the spring wind, past whose ear no rider was ever found dead

symbols.name: Sword Fragarach
symbols.meaning: 'The Answerer', a blade from his keeping that opened every fortress and from whose point no one escaped

symbols.name: Cloak of mist
symbols.meaning: The féth fíada, with which he hid the Otherworld and, in the Manx ballad, his whole island from pirates

symbols.name: The crane bag (corr bolg)
symbols.meaning: His crane-skin bag, which opened only when the tide was at the full — a purse that keeps the sea's clock

mythology.lead: Manannán moves through Irish myth like the tide: now distant, now suddenly present, always at the boundary between worlds. He is not a creator or a warrior king but the guardian of passages — between island and island, between the visible Ireland and the hidden one — and the keeper of the treasures that let a hero cross. His dossier spans the voyage-tale, the adventure-tale, the fosterage-tale, and the weapon-lore of the whole cycle.

myths.title: The Chariot on the Wave-Plain
myths.text:
In Immram Brain, the Voyage of Bran, the god meets a mortal expedition on its own element. Bran mac Febail had heard music behind him until he slept, and woke to find a silver branch with white blossoms at his hand; a strange woman sang to him of the Land of Women until he put to sea with three companies of nine. Out on the ocean a chariot came toward the boat, and the charioteer hailed Bran across the water — it was Manannán mac Lir, driving over what Bran took for the sea and the god took for a flowery plain. His chariot wheels were the chariot-wheels of the plain; the speckled salmon in the wave were calves and lambs to him; and from the driver's seat he sang the poem of the crossing, naming the islands Bran would pass and promising the harbour ahead.

The scene is the whole of his theology in one image: the crossing is not a change of place but of sight. What is sea to the mortal is meadow to the god, and the boat that labours through the wave is, from the far side, a chariot travelling home. Every immram is a lesson in looking twice at the water.

myths.title: The Silver Apples of the Land of Promise
myths.text:
Echtra Cormaic maic Airt i Tír Tairngiri sends him into Tara itself. A warrior appeared at Cormac mac Airt's court bearing a branch with three silver apples that played sweet music; for it the king gave, one by one, his wife and his son and his daughter — and then grieved. A grey-haired man with a shining branch led him through a mist into the Land of Promise, where four palaces stood and a pig was roasted and renewed every night, and where an aged couple kept an ever-full cauldron: 'the world is a wave,' the old man told him, 'ebbing and flowing.' Manannán showed him the cup of truth that split into three pieces when three lies were told beneath it, and when Cormac's own tale of loss proved true the cup healed whole again; then the god kept the true cup for himself and sent the king home with its likeness, his family riding behind him.

The tale is a merchant's ledger written as myth: every exchange cost exactly what it revealed. Cormac traded his dearest three for a music he could not keep, and was paid back only when his word was tested and found true — Manannán's commerce is never in gold but in the truth of the bargain.

myths.title: The Keeper of the Hollow Hills
myths.text:
Altram Tige Dá Medar, the Fosterage of the House of the Two Methers, gives him his strangest office: landlord of the gods. When the sons of Míl divided Ireland among mortals, Manannán counselled the Túatha Dé Danann not to contest the division but to take the sídhe — the hollow hills beneath the land — and he himself allotted each god his mound: the Dagda his Brug, Bodb Derg the síd of Munster, Midir his Brí Léith. He became foster-father to the children of the gods — [[aengus|Óengus]] among them — and his mist, the féth fíada, hid the hidden Ireland from human eyes. His own dwelling he kept apart, at Emain Ablach, the Isle of Apple-trees, in the sea to the west where no storm dies down.

The sea-god turns out to be the manager of the transition between sovereignties — the one power both peoples can deal with. Mortals inherit the surface; the gods retire to the hills; and Manannán, who belongs to neither element entirely, keeps the paperwork of both. He is the diplomat of the two Irelands, and the mist is his treaty.

myths.title: The Answerer, the Wave-Sweeper, and the Seven Pigs
myths.text:
His wealth is passage, and the cycle spends it everywhere. To Lugh, the tradition says, he gave the sword Fragarach, the Answerer, from whose point no one escaped and which opened every gate; his horse Aonbharr ran over land and sea alike; his boat Sguaba Tuinne answered thought and needed no sail; his crane-bag opened only at the full of the tide. In the late tale Oidheadh Chlainne Tuireann, Lugh's eric against his father's killers demands still more from the god's household: the seven pigs of Manannán, killed and eaten each night and found whole each morning, went on the quest-list, and the three sons of Tuireann won them with the rest. When the sons returned broken and died at Cian's grave, the treasures stayed in the world; the god's purse was never the poorer, because everything he lends comes home.

Read the inventory and the doctrine appears: there is no treasure of Manannán's that does not carry somebody somewhere. Sword, horse, boat, bag, pigs — even the cup of truth is a vessel. A god of the threshold gives only instruments of crossing, and keeps nothing but the sea.

lore.syncretism: Manannán's closest counterpart is the Welsh Manawydan fab Llŷr, the patient, just, sea-wise figure of the Second and Third Branches of the Mabinogi — husband of [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], and the one lord in the Welsh tales who cannot be outwitted or outwaited. Both names rest on a Common Celtic *Manaw-, and both bear the same patronymic: son of Lir, son of Llŷr, the Sea. The Isle of Man kept him longest: the Manx ballad of Mannan beg mac y Leir remembers him shrouding the island in mist to baffle pirates and levying his yearly tribute, and the island's name itself is his monument. The medieval chronicles euhemerized him into an early sea-king, a demotion the folklore never ratified. Roman-period sea-god dedications around the western coasts give a wider maritime context, but no inscription names him, and the comparisons remain structural.
lore.culturalLegacy: He left his name on the Isle of Man and on a working relationship with its people that outlasted belief: the Manx kept paying 'Manannán's rent' and telling his ballad into the modern period, and a landmark statue of the sea-lord now looks out over Lough Foyle from Binevenagh's heights. Ireland's coastal folklore kept him as the guardian of the waters, and the Irish-language revival and the Celtic Twilight restored him to literature. In the material world he sails still: the Isle of Man Steam Packet's fastest craft is named Manannán, a theonym crossing the Irish Sea three times a day. Neopaganism honours him as lord of sea and Otherworld, and fantasy literature — from Lord Dunsany's haunted western isles to a shelf of novels and games — keeps the mist, the boat, and the horse that runs on water.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Manannán is the god of the horizon. He does not rule the land; he rules the mist that hides the land beyond the land, and his household — the Answerer, the Wave-Sweeper, the horse Aonbharr, the crane-bag — is an inventory of crossings. To meet him is to discover that the boundary you thought was an end is actually a door: the sea that separates Ireland from Tír na nÓg is the same sea that brings the fog, the fish, and the stranger.

That is why his great scenes are all acts of explanation. From the driver's seat of his chariot he re-describes the ocean to Bran until it becomes a meadow; from the Land of Promise he teaches Cormac that the world is a wave, ebbing and flowing; and from the threshold of the sídhe he manages the gods' retreat into the hills so precisely that both Irelands survive the exchange. He asks us to become navigators of uncertainty: to trust the invisible road, to accept the cloak of mist, and to remember that every shore is someone else's threshold — and that the tide, which looks like an ending twice a day, is the oldest promise of return in the world.

lore.archaeology: No inscription names Manannán directly, and the temple is honest that his evidence is textual and onomastic. The Isle of Man's name is the durable monument: late-antique geographers knew the island as Monapia, and the Manx Mannin preserves the element, whatever its first meaning. The material culture of Irish seafaring — the currach tradition, the promontory forts, the votive deposits in rivers and bogs — frames the cult but cannot be tied to him. Romano-British altars to maritime powers along the western coasts give a comparative backdrop, not an identification. The manuscript record is the real archaeology: Immram Brain survives in the twelfth-century Lebor na hUidre and later copies, Echtra Cormaic in the late vellum manuscripts, and the fosterage-tale in the great codices of the mythological cycle.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in medieval Irish manuscripts in the Insular Latin script as Manannán, with the síneadh fada marking the long á — the very feature that makes the restoration Tier 1 — while the Manx and Welsh branches write their own forms (Mannan, Manawydan). The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. The temple's domain manannán.com carries the fada itself — a Unicode domain registered in the PuniCodex collection, routed at the edge to /sites/manannan/ alongside its punycode form xn--manannn-mwa.com.
